newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Timorese in French embassy to leave for Portugal.
newsitem.headline: Timorese in French embassy to leave for Portugal.

text.p: Three East Timorese men who broke into the French embassy in Jakarta early on Tuesday will leave for political asylum in Portugal later in the day, diplomatic sources said.
The three scaled the three-metre (nine-foot) high spiked iron fence surrounding the French embassy compound and waved a banner saying "Free East Timor" while shouting "Viva East Timor".
"They will go to asylum in Portugal later this afternoon," a diplomatic source said.
Indonesian Foreign Ministry spokesman Ghaffar Fadyl said delegates from the Jakarta office of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) had visited the French embassy after the break-in.
The Geneva-based ICRC has facilitated the travel of 93 East Timorese who have fled their troubled homeland and sought asylum in foreign embassies in Jakarta since September 1995.
"As usual, after the proper procedures have been done, they can go," Fadyl told Reuters.
East Timorese sources said the three were seeking asylum in Portugal after being involved in a protest in the East Timor capital Dili on November 25.

A letter listing 10 demands on behalf of those seeking asylum, faxed to Reuters, appeared to suggest the men had planned to enter the nearby Spanish embassy as the three-page document dated December 3 is addressed to the Spanish ambassador.

Soon after they entered the compound at about 6 a.m. (2300 GMT Monday) a French official arrived and spoke to them. The three men handed over their identity cards, folded their banner and put it in a backpack that one of the men was carrying.

The French embassy, which recently raised its spiked iron fence, has been a particular target of break-ins. The latest is the ninth since November 1995. French diplomats refused to comment on the case when contacted on Tuesday.
Three East Timorese who were seen in the mission compound after a break-in on October 16 later said they were thrown out of the premises by an embassy official.
At the time French embassy officials refused to acknowledge that any East Timorese had entered their mission.
The letter calls for greater involvement of the United Nations in East Timor and a referendum over the future of the territory which Indonesia invaded on December 7, 1975.

Following the Indonesian invasion, Jakarta annexed East Timor, a former Portuguese colony, in July 1976 in an act not recognised by the United Nations. Many East Timorese oppose Jakarta's rule and accuse Indonesian troops in the territory of human rights abuses.
